short: one physical copy of a row. an UPDATE writes a new one and leaves the old one on the page.
the id of the transaction that wrote a tuple version. a system column on every row.
the id of the transaction that deleted, updated or locked a tuple version. 0 if nobody has.
the header field that points from an old tuple version to the one that replaced it. the newest points at itself.
a tuple version no snapshot can see anymore. it takes up space until VACUUM or pruning removes it.
a built-in trigger function that skips an UPDATE when the new row equals the old one.
the 32-bit number a transaction gets at its first write. it goes into xmin and xmax of the tuples it touches.
the cheap id every transaction holds from its first statement: backend number / local counter. never written to disk.
xmin, xmax and the list of transactions in progress when it was taken. decides whose changes a query can see.
the fixed series of tests on a tuple's xmin, xmax, the commit log and a snapshot that decides if a reader sees that version.
the commit log: two bits per transaction id saying in progress, committed, aborted or sub-committed.
commit status flags a reader writes into a tuple header after looking it up in pg_xact, so the next reader doesn't have to.
an UPDATE whose new version stays on the same page with no indexed column changed, so no index entry is written.
cleanup of dead versions inside one page, done by any statement that reads a nearly full page. no VACUUM needed.
a line pointer left at the root of a pruned HOT chain, pointing at the chain's live version so index entries keep working.
rewrites a table and its indexes into new files, giving space back, under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.
space a table or index takes beyond what its live rows need: dead tuples and free space not yet reused.
the background launcher and workers that vacuum and analyze tables once enough rows changed.
the oldest snapshot xmin or xid anything still holds. versions deleted after it can't be removed yet.
marking a tuple as older than every transaction, so wraparound can't make it disappear. two infomask bits.
32-bit transaction ids run round a circle; an unfrozen tuple more than 2 billion behind would look like the future.
an id standing for several transactions that lock one row at once, stored in xmax. its own 32-bit counter.
where InnoDB and oracle keep old values after updating rows in place. readers rebuild old versions from it.
